uncited: Sampling and Integration Schemes define the computational framework for evaluating the volume rendering equation along a viewing ray, converting discrete volumetric data into a final pixel color.
This family encompasses methods that determine *where* to sample the volume (stochastic vs. deterministic spacing) and *how* to aggregate those samples (compositing, projection, or approximation).

It is distinguished from [Interpolation and Sampling Techniques](2787-interpolation-and-sampling-techniques.md) by focusing on the integration logic and sampling distribution rather than the spatial interpolation kernel, and from [Ray Marching and Discretization](2788-ray-marching-and-discretization.md) by encompassing both the sampling strategy and the reduction phase.
All methods in this family operate on the principle that a continuous function $V(\mathbf{p})$ must be approximated from a discrete set of samples $V_i$ located at grid positions $\mathbf{p}_i$.
**Query Positioning**: Determining the 3D coordinate $\mathbf{p}$ along the ray $r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ where a value is needed.
This may involve converting depth parameters to physical distances or warping coordinates for neural encodings.
**Kernel/Weight Application**: Computing weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$ based on the distance between $\mathbf{p}$ and the sample centers $\mathbf{p}_i$.
The choice of kernel (e.g., linear, cubic, inverse distance) determines the spatial extent (number of neighbors) and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) .
**Coordinate Transformation**: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the local coordinate system of the volume data (e.g., normalized $[-1, 1]$ or $[0, 1]$ ranges) before interpolation .
The family originates from the fundamental volume rendering equation formulated by Williams et al. .
Early implementations relied on uniform sampling and front-to-back compositing .
Monte Carlo methods were adapted from photon mapping techniques to handle participating media .
Pre-integration was introduced to address the "missing peak" problem in transfer functions .
